Summary

One idea at two scales: keep a compact state of a partially observed history and answer several questions from it. Part 1 learns that state on business-process event logs. Part 2 builds the loop that turns live agent runs into training data, trains small models, and puts them back into the agent.

+7% vs +95%
Part 1: error increase under an honest temporal shift, learned state (GRU) vs gradient-boosted trees. In-distribution they tie.
70.7% / 76.7%
Part 1: accuracy under the published BPI 2013 protocol vs 64.0% / 74.7% best published (Closed Problems / Incidents).
27 → 29 → 30 / 30
Part 2: Opus 5 on held-out AppWorld dev tasks: raw → with a persistent world frame → with a forked oracle picker. The learned picker holds 29/30 at half the invalid actions.
The connection. An AppWorld episode is converted into a Part 1 case (API call = event, error = attribute, outcome = terminal event) and the Part 1 model is one of the two learned components reinserted into the agent. The world frame in Part 2 is the same idea with text instead of 128 numbers, because the reader is an LLM.

Part 1 — What it is for

Given the first events of a business case (an IT ticket, an expense claim), predict what happens next, when, and how it ends, from one model that updates as events arrive, with honest uncertainty, and that stays useful when the process or its vocabulary changes.

The data

Eight public XES event logs. BPI 2013 (Volvo IT): Incidents (7,554 tickets), Closed Problems, Open Problems. BPI 2020 (university travel expenses): Domestic Declarations, International Declarations, Prepaid Travel Costs, Request for Payment, Permit Log. Each case is an ordered list of timestamped events with attributes (team, role, person, severity, product; or amounts and roles).

The questions asked at every prefix

  • Next activity (with an explicit "end of case" class)
  • Time to the next event as a distribution, so intervals not just points
  • Remaining time to the end, which also yields "probability still open in 7 days"
  • The whole remaining suffix by rolling the model forward
Why it matters. Operational systems emit partial histories, not fixed-size examples. A model that must re-read the whole history per event does not scale, and a model that only answers one question needs a sibling per question. The claim tested: one compact per-case state can serve all four questions and survive distribution shift better than a stateless model over hand-made prefix features.

What the audit found before modelling

A streaming parser keeps every column raw; bpm/ingest/audit.py computes the claims; bpm/ingest/registry.py records per log which fields are activity, input, excluded (with the reason), which activities are real endings, and whether the log is censored.

  • Incidents is a snapshot: 96% of cases start within six weeks of 2012 and 98% of Closed events were bulk-closed in one May batch. 25% of tickets never close.
  • PermitLog columns dec_id_* / TotalDeclared have mutual information 1.0 with the outcome: filled in after the fact. Excluded.
  • org:resource is a person in BPI 2013 and an anonymised token (STAFF MEMBER / SYSTEM) in BPI 2020: same field name, different meaning across families.
  • Rule adopted: a case is complete only if its last activity is in the log's terminal set. Suffix and remaining-time targets come only from complete cases; next-event targets from every prefix; Open Problems is censored wholesale.

Part 1 — How it works

Event → vector
activity embedding + Σ embeddings of its decomposed parts (e.g. Declaration / APPROVED / SUPERVISOR) + one embedding per attribute (rare values → UNK) + 7 time features on log scale
→
State
2-layer GRU, 128 numbers, rewritten on every event (O(1) per event). Alternative: 2-layer causal Transformer, KV cache as the state. Same heads.
→
Three heads
softmax over activities incl. END · 3-component Gaussian mixture on log Δt · Laplace on log remaining time
→
Rollout
feed predictions back in until END; greedy, or the medoid of 5 samples

Training choices

  • Loss = CE + 0.5·NLL(Δt) + 0.5·NLL(remaining), weights fixed before any test run.
  • 15% of attributes randomly blanked during training, so multi-step rollouts (which have no attributes for imagined events) stay in-distribution.
  • AdamW, up to 60 epochs, early stop on validation, three seeds. 214k parameters; seconds per epoch on a laptop CPU.
  • Vocabularies, rare-value thresholds and time scalers are fit on training cases only and saved as JSON next to the results.

Baselines, identical preprocessing

  • Markov k=2: next-activity table conditioned on the last two activities with back-off; per-context median times.
  • Gradient-boosted trees (sklearn): last 3 activities, activity counts so far, time features, current attributes; one classifier and two absolute-error regressors; autoregressive rollout.

Purpose: tell whether the learned state adds anything over counting and over a strong stateless model.

Why these specific decisions
  • END as an activity: termination becomes a prediction, not a heuristic; rollouts stop by themselves.
  • Decomposed labels: a renamed step still shares parts with known steps; this is also what allows cross-log transfer with a union vocabulary.
  • Mixture on log Δt: gaps span minutes to months and are multi-modal (same day vs next working day); one Gaussian cannot represent that.
  • Laplace for remaining time: a Gaussian head diverged on long-tailed logs; the Laplace point estimate is the median and its survival function gives SLA risk directly.
  • GRU over Transformer as the main model: same accuracy, constant memory per case, and the Transformer's longer memory did not translate into accuracy (see findings).

Part 1 — How it was tested

SplitWhat it testsHow it is built
Random 70/15/15In-distribution accuracyWhole cases shuffled with a fixed seed; validation only for early stopping and temperature.
Chronological, leakyWhat most papers call a temporal splitCases sorted by start; cut at 70%; training cases kept whole even if they run past the cutoff (67% of Incidents train cases overlap the test window).
Chronological, strictHonest "train on the past, test on the future"Training events after the cutoff deleted; truncated cases marked incomplete.
Published 5-fold CVComparability with published BPI 2013 numbersSame protocol as the papers, incomplete cases assumed complete; activity-only Markov as the sanity check.
Transfer RfP → DomesticVocabulary / process changeTrain on Request for Payment, test on all of Domestic Declarations; union vocabulary; fine-tune vs scratch at equal budget.
Attribute-removal probeRobustness when inputs disappearEvery trained model re-scored with all event attributes masked at test time.

Metrics. Next activity: NLL, accuracy, macro-F1, ECE and Brier (raw and temperature-scaled). Times: MAE and median AE in hours, interval coverage. Suffix: normalised Damerau–Levenshtein similarity, exact match, valid termination rate. Everything with 95% case-level bootstrap intervals and three training seeds.

Part 1 — What the results show

  1. In distribution a stateless tree ties a learned state on the large logs and beats it on the attribute-rich Incidents log. Reason found by ablation: the tree splits directly on the 472-value team field, while the GRU squeezes it through an 8-dimensional embedding into a 128-number state. Not caused by attribute dropout or capacity (both tested).
  2. Under an honest temporal shift the state wins decisively. Incidents strict: GBM +95% NLL (accuracy 0.77 → 0.57, suffix similarity halved), GRU +7%, Transformer +8%. The leaky split hides this. How you split matters more than which model.
  3. Robustness to missing inputs follows from attribute dropout: GBM +69% vs GRU +23% when attributes are masked.
  4. Decoding beats architecture for coherence. Greedy rollouts loop; medoid decoding terminates every time and lifts suffix similarity above the tree.
  5. Calibrated out of the box, and selective prediction is a usable downstream product. Seed-ensemble uncertainty does not detect shift.
  6. Published protocol reproduced, both learned models above every published row; the margin comes largely from event attributes, since the activity-only baseline lands in the published range.
  7. Longer memory does not help here. A KL probe shows the GRU forgets an early rejection within ~3 events (≤ 0.01 nats) while the Transformer retains it at 6–10 events (0.03–0.04), yet accuracy is equal. After FINAL_APPROVED, 99.1% of 9,145 prefixes proceed normally and nothing in the prefix separates the rest: the residual error is caused by information outside the log.
  8. Errors compound. After the first wrong event, 90–93% of the rest of a greedy suffix is wrong, for both state designs. Remaining-time predictions are non-monotone at 13–33% of positions.

Part 2 — What it is for

A benchmark-agnostic loop: run an LLM agent in an interactive environment, record complete versioned traces, turn them into training examples, train a small model, put it back into the agent so it changes behaviour, and compare against the original agent on held-out tasks. AppWorld is the first adapter.

AppWorld

A simulated phone with nine apps (Spotify, Venmo, Gmail, Amazon, Splitwise, Todoist, phone, file system, notes) behind ~450 Python APIs, and 750 tasks phrased as a supervisor's request ("send this message to my roommates who don't have Venmo"). The agent writes Python that calls apis.<app>.<api>(...), sees the output, repeats. Each task ships hidden unit tests over the final app state; a task passes when all tests pass (TGC); a scenario passes when all three variants pass (SGC).

The learned role: a picker

The LLM proposes N=3 code blocks per step; a small model chooses one; only that one executes. Two learned scorers with different blind spots, rule-based gates as controls, and an environment-forking oracle as the ceiling. The LLM never stops writing the code; the learned part only selects.

Why a picker. It is the smallest role that closes the loop honestly: a model trained on this environment's outcomes changes what the agent executes, is measurable against a no-picker baseline and a perfect-picker oracle, uses samples that would otherwise be discarded, and is a cost dial (N=1 is the baseline). It is also the data-collection step of rejection sampling / RL on the generator, which is the version that scales.

Part 2 — How it works

Environment contract
task_ids · reset · step · action_schema · evaluate · version. AppWorld runs as a server in its own venv (pydantic 1) and is driven over HTTP; a 60-line mock world implements the same contract.
→
Agent
Claude (Haiku 4.5, then Opus 5) writes one Python block per turn; versioned prompts v1–v4 hashed into every trace; memory = raw history window or the world frame.
→
Policy
choose(context, candidates): first-candidate (baseline), token scorer, trace model, hybrid, oracle; optional gates in front.
→
Trace
one validated, redacted JSON line per episode; checker called after every step; every candidate's forked outcome recorded.

What a trace holds (schema 1.1.0)

Ids (env, benchmark, task, scenario, episode, run), split, versions (AppWorld, model, prompt hash, git sha, policy, seed), per step: observation, action-schema hash, all candidates (raw reply, parsed action, tokens, score, counterfactual outcome), chosen index, tool result, typed error, reward (Δ checker passes), evaluator output, latency and cost; termination reason; final evaluation. Failed actions stay. Every training example carries provenance to (file, episode, step, candidate).

Redaction (v2) and hygiene

Values of secret-named keys, any code assignment or argument whose name contains a secret word (including strings cut off by the token limit), and JWT-shaped blobs become <REDACTED:salted-hash> at write time; idempotent. Rules v1 missed three shapes; a pre-release scan of all 1,625 committed episodes found them (all AppWorld synthetic values) and every trace was re-redacted. Collection on train tasks only; evaluation on 30 dev tasks × 2 runs; the test split was never touched.

Labels from the environment (the FDM-1 borrowings)

  • Checker after every step. Reward = tests passed now minus before. A step that raises the count is progress; one that lowers it, or calls "done" while tests still fail, is regress. Credit lands on the step that caused it instead of one bit per episode.
  • Fork every candidate. Snapshot the world (database checkpoint + Python-namespace snapshot), run candidate 1, grade, roll back; same for 2 and 3. All three samples get real outcomes: 3× the rows, and contrastive (same context, different code, different result). 0.3 s per step; verified equal to full replay.
  • Oracle picker. Once all three are tried for real, keep the one the checker rewards most. Not a method (needs the checker at test time); the ceiling for any learned picker.
Forking and per-step grading are training-time only. On dev tasks the learned picker predicts from context + code with no forking and no checker. The oracle arm is the one exception and is reported as an upper bound.

Part 2 — Learned components

Token scorerTrace world model
Seesthe candidate's code + last observation + last error as hashed word/char n-grams, plus step index and error countthe episode as a sequence of app.api|ok/err events with START and OUTCOME pseudo-events; the candidate as its first API call
Modellogistic regression, 2¹⁸ hashed features, class-balanced; seconds on CPUthe Part 1 GRU, trained on episodes converted to cases
OutputsP(valid), P(progress), P(regress), P(episode success)validity = P(api|ok)/(P(ok)+P(err)), plausibility = P(api next), success by rolling out to OUTCOME_OK
Blind spotno memory of earlier stepsarguments: a right and a wrong call to the same API look identical
Offline, held-out scenariosvalid AUROC 0.965, progress 0.99, regress 1.00next-API top-1 0.43, validity 0.82, outcome 0.75

Policies. baseline executes the first sample. reranker ranks by P(valid)·(0.5+P(progress))·(1−P(regress)). tracemodel ranks by validity·plausibility·success; with --validity-model it becomes the hybrid (multiplied by the token scorer, so either can veto). --gate drops candidates that call APIs absent from the schema or call "done" before the checker is satisfied. oracle uses the forked outcomes.

Part 2 — World frame PERSIST-style explicit state, used with Opus 5

The raw agent conditions on a window of its last 12 turns of code and output. The world frame replaces most of that with a compact, explicitly updated state block rendered at the top of every prompt: the Part 1 idea (keep a state, don't re-read history) with text instead of numbers because the reader is an LLM.

Contents

  • apps involved in the task
  • per app: API names known, signatures of any whose docs were read
  • which Python variable holds each app's token
  • entity summaries from JSON outputs (count, id field, first ids, keys)
  • last error per API (so it is not repeated)
  • free-text note("…") lines the agent chose to keep

Lifecycle

  • Seeded before step 1: apps implied by the task text get their full API list from the published schema plus the login signature (PERSIST's explicit initialisation, their best ablation).
  • Updated after every step by regexes over the code and its output. Deterministic, no model.
  • Rendered as a fixed-cost block; raw history cut from 12 to 4 turns.
Why it rescued a whole scenario (checked in all 12 episodes)

Task 50e1ac9: "top 4 most played R&B songs across my Spotify song, album and playlist libraries." Spotify has show_song_library / show_album_library (what the task means) and a separate show_liked_songs / show_liked_albums. Raw Opus, all six attempts: read a 40-entry API description dump, then picked the liked APIs, collected 59 songs, missed one title, failed. World frame, all six attempts: picked the library APIs, 79 songs, correct, 6 steps instead of 10. The compact API list sat next to the task text at the moment of choosing; the raw agent had seen the same names once, in a dump that scrolled out of its window. The benefit was the map being in view, not memory across steps.

Training data: what each picker was trained on

AppWorld ships four task splits: train 90, dev 57, test-normal 168, test-challenge 417 (30 / 19 / 56 / 139 scenarios × 3 variants). Collection used the train split only; the pickers were evaluated on 30 dev tasks; the test splits were never run. Held-out for the offline metrics = whole scenarios held out from the training collection, so no variant of a training scenario leaks into its own offline test.

Part 2 — What the results show

  1. The generator was the whole Haiku story. Same harness, tasks and seeds go from ≤ 6.7% to 90% by swapping the model. The oracle is what proved it: even with the environment as judge, best-of-3 was flat.
  2. The persistent state adds two tasks per run and cuts cost 28%. It rescues an entire scenario the raw agent fails six times out of six, by keeping the API map in view. Its cost is more exploratory errors (invalid 4.2% → 9.5%): with API names pre-listed the agent skips reading docs and guesses signatures.
  3. The learned picker buys efficiency, not correctness. On top of the world frame it keeps 29/30 while halving invalid actions (9.5% → 4.9%) and shortening episodes (9.4 → 8.8 steps), for 2.8× the LLM cost. It removed exactly the signature errors the frame introduced.
  4. Selection is worth the gap between the generator's menu and the checker's optimum. Nothing when the menu is empty (Haiku); efficiency when the menu is good (Opus); the last episode only with the environment in the loop (oracle).
  5. Offline-vs-online gap, two concrete instances. A validity-only picker prefers a bare complete_task() because it never errors (19/60 Haiku episodes ended within two steps); and the API-level trace model cannot see argument mistakes the text model can. Strong offline AUROCs (0.97–1.00) translated into fewer errors, not more solved tasks.
Caveat, stated up front. Every Opus difference except the scenario rescue is one or two episodes in 30. The picker's two misses are in a scenario the raw agent solves every time, and the oracle's overrides there only avoided erroring candidates (no candidate changed the checker's count). Two runs cannot separate 29/30 from 30/30. Next step is five seeds.

Limitations & next steps

Limitations

  • Part 1: the GRU loses to the tree in-distribution on Incidents (high-cardinality team field through a small embedding). The remaining-time head is non-monotone at 13–33% of positions. Seed-ensemble uncertainty does not detect shift.
  • Part 2: 30 dev tasks × 2 runs; differences of one episode are inside the noise. The picker triples LLM cost. The trace model is API-level and blind to arguments. Per-step grading and forking need a checker and a restorable environment; without one the pipeline degrades to validity labels from tracebacks (AUROC 0.965 alone), and unverifiable tasks need a grader or human labels.
  • Only one real benchmark adapter was exercised; the world-frame seeding relies on a keyword table that may be AppWorld-shaped.

Next steps, in order

  1. Five seeds on the Opus arms with a task-level bootstrap.
  2. A second benchmark adapter (tau-bench or a WebArena subset) to test the agnostic claim and the world frame.
  3. Score one sample and resample only when the score is low (most of the error reduction at ~1.3× cost).
  4. Argument-aware picker features: does each argument value appear in an earlier output or the frame.
  5. A learned progress estimator (checker Δ from prefix + candidate) to replace forking at test time; the counterfactual dataset already has the labels.
  6. Part 1: larger or hashed inputs for the high-cardinality fields; a survival-style remaining-time head.
  7. Long term: RL on an open-weight generator from these traces.

Reproduce

Python 3.12 via uv; uv.lock pins everything. Verified from a fresh clone: 19 tests, Part 1 demo in ~10 s, Part 2 offline demo with no API key.

uv sync --extra dev
make test                       # 19 tests: splits, targets, streaming state, schema, redaction, train→reinsert, forking, world frame
make audit                      # data audit, all 8 logs → results/audit/
make demo                       # Part 1 one-command demo → results/demo.json
make demo-part2                 # Part 2 collect → dataset → train → reinsert on the mock world
scripts/run_all_part1.sh        # all Part 1 configs (~1 h) then: uv run python -m bpm.report
make appworld-setup             # optional: AppWorld in its own venv (needs ~200 MB data)
scripts/run_part2_v4.sh         # Opus 5 arms as run (needs ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in .env)
